section.title: The Useless Vine
section.sectionRationale: Israel had long pictured herself as God's chosen vine, but Ezekiel strips away every illusion of inherent value in the vine's own wood. Unlike sturdy timber, vine wood is useless for anything but bearing fruit; charred by fire and fruitless, Jerusalem has become good for nothing at all except further burning, a brief, brutal parable that clears the ground for the fuller vine and bride imagery to come.
section.thesis: The wood of a vine has no worth in itself, no strength for building, no use as a peg, its entire value lies in bearing fruit; so Jerusalem, having borne no fruit of faithfulness and having already been scorched once by judgment, is fit only to be consumed further, a warning that finds its full resolution only in the true, fruitful vine, Jesus Christ, and the branches that abide in Him.
section.frameNote: Two movements: the vine's inherent uselessness apart from fruit, even when whole, unable to serve as timber or a simple peg; and the direct application of that uselessness to Jerusalem, already touched by one fire and now given over to another.

units.label: Wood good for nothing
units.note: the vine's uselessness apart from fruit

verses.text: Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying,
“Son of man, how does the wood of the {{gephen|vine}} surpass any other branch among the trees in the forest?
Can wood be taken from it to make something useful? Or can one make from it a peg on which to hang utensils?
No, it is cast into the fire for fuel. The fire devours both ends, and the middle is charred. Can it be useful for anything?
Even when it was whole, it could not be made useful. How much less can it ever be useful when the fire has consumed it and charred it!
Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Like the wood of the vine among the trees of the forest, which I have given to the fire for fuel, so I will give up the people of Jerusalem.
And I will set My face against them. Though they may have escaped the fire, yet another fire will consume them. And when I set My face against them, you will know that I am the LORD.
Thus I will make the land desolate, because they have acted {{maal|unfaithfully}},’ declares the Lord GOD.”

gephen.gloss: Vine. Israel is repeatedly pictured as God's vine or vineyard, Psalm 80:8-16, Isaiah 5:1-7, Hosea 10:1; here the image is stripped of all sentiment, focusing solely on the wood's uselessness apart from bearing fruit.

maal.gloss: Treachery, unfaithfulness, a breach of trust, often used of covenant betrayal. The land's desolation is directly tied to this ma'al, the same term used elsewhere in Scripture for Israel's persistent covenant infidelity.

basic.context: Israel loved to picture itself as God's vine, a symbol of privilege and promise. Ezekiel dismantles that comfort with a blunt question: apart from fruit, what is vine wood actually good for? Not even a peg. Having already been scorched once by judgment and still bearing no fruit, Jerusalem is fit only for further burning.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a short, sharp parable applied directly and explicitly to Jerusalem by God Himself in verse 6, not left open to interpretation. Its plain, uncomfortable point is that privilege without fruit carries no independent value; being the vine means everything if it bears fruit, and nothing at all if it does not.
basic.originalLanguages: The gephen, vine, was Israel's favorite self-image across the Psalms and Prophets, but here its wood is shown structurally worthless apart from fruit-bearing, unlike timber trees prized for their wood itself. The land's coming desolation is tied to Israel's ma'al, unfaithfulness, a term elsewhere describing serious covenant betrayal, not a minor lapse.
basic.typology: The useless, fruitless vine cast into the fire anticipates Jesus' own words in John 15:1-6, where He identifies Himself as 'the true vine' and warns that any branch not abiding in Him and bearing fruit 'is thrown away and withers... thrown into the fire and burned', a direct echo and fulfillment of this exact image.
basic.christ: Where Jerusalem, the failed vine, could only be judged and burned for its fruitlessness, Jesus presents Himself as the true and faithful vine, John 15:1, in whom His people, as branches, can finally bear the fruit Israel could not produce on her own; apart from Him people remain like this useless wood, but abiding in Him, much fruit is genuinely possible.
basic.god: God is unsentimental about privilege detached from fruitfulness; being chosen as His vine carries real responsibility, not automatic protection, and He will not spare a fruitless people simply because of their favored status or history.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 80:8-16 pictures Israel as a vine brought out of Egypt. Isaiah 5:1-7 tells the song of the vineyard that yielded only wild grapes. Hosea 10:1 calls Israel a luxuriant vine. John 15:1-6 has Jesus declare Himself the true vine whose fruitless branches are burned.
basic.oneStory: This is the collapse of Israel's favorite self-image, a vine whose wood, apart from fruit, is worth nothing at all. The story does not end with fruitless wood destined for the fire; it runs forward to Jesus, the true vine, who makes genuine fruitfulness possible for every branch that abides in Him.

context.literary:
Ezekiel 15 is the shortest sustained unit in this stretch of the book, only eight verses, and it is a model of compression. It follows the plain two-step shape of a prophetic parable: an image in verses 2 to 5, and an application introduced by 'Therefore' in verses 6 to 8. What makes it unusual is that the image is not a story but a string of questions. Verse 2 asks how vine wood surpasses other wood, verse 3 asks whether anything useful can be made from it, and verse 4 asks the last question, 'Can it be useful for anything?' The prophet gives the answer before the hearer can supply it. The grammar of the questions expects the answer 'no,' and the audience is led to say it themselves.

The argument is a fortiori, from the lesser to the greater. Verse 5 says that even when the wood was 'whole' it could not be made into anything, and then asks how much less once the fire has charred it. The whole structure hangs on that contrast between whole and burned, which the application picks up in verse 7: 'Though they may have escaped the fire, yet another fire will consume them.' The two fires in the application match the two states of the wood in the image, and they are the chapter's sharpest riddle.

The chapter's place is also significant. It comes between the exposure of false prophets and idolatrous elders in chapters 13 and 14 and the long marriage allegory of chapter 16, and it bridges them by moving from leaders to the city as a whole. It also begins a run of images drawn from nature and family, the vine here, the bride in chapter 16, the eagles and the vine again in chapter 17, the lioness in chapter 19. Each takes a cherished picture of Israel and turns it against her. The brevity of this one makes it the hinge between the long indictments around it.
context.historical:
To the exiles, the vine was among the proudest images of their national identity. Israel had been brought out of Egypt like a vine, Psalm 80:8. The grapevine was one of the great fruits of the land that Moses' spies carried back, and a clustered vine was a symbol of the land's abundance. When the prophets spoke of Israel as God's vine, they were using a flattering image that every worshiper knew from the psalms. Ezekiel starts from that pride and presses on one point: apart from its fruit, vine wood is useless.

The practical facts behind the question are accurate to the craft of the time. A vine is a trailing, twisting plant whose stems are crooked and short, not suitable for timber. Builders did not use it for beams, and the peg of verse 3 is a tent peg or wall peg for hanging things, a small, humble object, mentioned in Isaiah 22:23-25 where a peg holds a load. Even that modest use is denied to vine wood. It could only be burned, and after burning even less could be done with it.

The application is aimed at a particular moment. In 597 BC the first deportation took Jehoiachin and the leading men to Babylon, and Jerusalem was left standing with Zedekiah on the throne. The people left behind took their survival as a sign of favor. Ezekiel 11:15 quotes what they said of the exiles: 'They are far away from the LORD; this land has been given to us as a possession.' The charred vine of verse 4 is the first fire, those who were taken, and the 'another fire' of verse 7 is the coming siege, which would burn Jerusalem in 586 BC, Jeremiah 52:12-13. The people who thought they had escaped had only been passed over for a time.
context.canonical:
The vine is one of Scripture's main pictures of Israel, and Ezekiel 15 is the point where its fortunes turn. Psalm 80:8-16 celebrates the vine brought from Egypt and pleads over it after it has been cut down and burned. Isaiah 5:1-7 sings a love song about a vineyard planted on a fertile hill that yields sour fruit, and in verse 5 the LORD says he will take away its hedge and let it be trampled. Jeremiah 2:21 says God planted a choice vine from the very best seed and asks how it turned into a 'rotten, wild vine.' Hosea 10:1 calls Israel a luxuriant vine that used its fruit for the altars of other gods. Ezekiel contributes the most blunt of these, a vine whose wood is not even worth a peg.

The prophet then returns to the vine in chapter 17, where Zedekiah's kingdom is a low spreading vine, Ezekiel 17:6, and in chapter 19, where the vine's strong branches are stripped and fire consumes its fruit, 19:12-14. The sequence shows how the same image is used for judgment, for politics and for lament.

The New Testament picks up the image. Jesus gives a parable of a landowner who plants a vineyard, Matthew 21:33-43, and tells the leaders that the kingdom will be given to a people who produce its fruit. He tells of a fig tree that bears nothing, Luke 13:6-9. John the Baptist warns that every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire, Matthew 3:10. Finally Jesus says in John 15:1, 'I am the true vine,' and in verse 6 uses the burning of fruitless branches. The line from Ezekiel 15 to John 15 is plain: God's people were always meant to be known by fruit.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Ezekiel's aim was to break a form of reasoning that the survivors in Jerusalem and the exiles in Babylon had in common. Both groups assumed that a people with a special status and a surviving remnant of that status was safe. The parable cuts that argument at its base by asking what makes a vine valuable. It is not the vine's rank among trees, verse 2, nor its wood, verse 3, but what it bears. A vine that bears no fruit has no other function to fall back on, and the people God planted for the sake of fruit are in the same position.

The parable has a second intent, aimed at the survivors of the first fire. Verse 7 says that having escaped one fire does not guarantee escape from another. Ezekiel wanted to dismantle the false comfort of those who read their deliverance in 597 as God's approval. A narrow escape is not a verdict. It may be a postponement.

The parable ends in a single reason, given without softening in verse 8: 'because they have acted unfaithfully.' The cause is not bad luck or bad politics. Ezekiel wanted his hearers to trace the coming disaster to its moral and covenant root. And since the vine is God's own, the chapter is addressed to people who still had time to ask what kind of fruit they were bearing. He means it as a warning and, by implication, a summons to the fruitfulness the vine was made for.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This is a parable that God Himself interprets in verse 6, so its meaning is fixed by the passage and not left to the reader. It describes how God judged Jerusalem. It does not prescribe a method for dealing with unproductive people, and it does not say that God measures human beings by their usefulness. The vine is useless as timber, and the point is made about a nation that was chosen to bear fruit, not about the worth of an individual who struggles or fails.

Care is needed in applying it. It would distort the passage to read it as a ranking of people by output or as proof that anyone who is weak will be discarded. The Bible says elsewhere that God honors the weak, 1 Corinthians 1:27, and Jesus received the sick and sinners. The charge in Ezekiel 15 is covenant unfaithfulness, a settled refusal to bear the fruit God had made possible, which is a different thing from weakness.

What carries forward is that privilege and fruitfulness belong together. A congregation or a believer can lean on a heritage, a baptism, a confession or a past experience as if it were a guarantee. The passage says that such things are valuable only for the fruit they are given to produce. Paul draws the same conclusion in Romans 11:20-22, telling the grafted branches not to be arrogant but to continue in God's kindness. Yet the New Testament also tells us the source of the fruit, which is union with Christ, John 15:5.

debates.question: What are the two fires of verse 7?

views.label: The first deportation and the final destruction
views.case: The fire that has already charred the vine is the capture of Jerusalem in 597 BC and the exile of Jehoiachin and the leading men, and the 'another fire' is the siege and burning of 586 BC. The people left behind who thought they had been spared are told the burning is not finished. This reading fits the context of Ezekiel 11:15 and the date of the book's early oracles.

views.label: Earlier judgments in Israel's history and the coming one
views.case: Others take the first fire more broadly, as the series of calamities that had already fallen on Israel, such as the fall of the northern kingdom and the earlier invasions. The point then is that earlier judgments had not purified the nation and a further one was still to come.

debates.bearing: Both readings give the same warning: a previous brush with disaster is not a guarantee against the next one. The text speaks of an 'escape' that was only provisional, and so it asks the survivors to treat what they have survived as a call to change, not as a sign of immunity.

debates.question: Is the vine condemned for what it is or for what it fails to do?

views.label: For what it is, wood that is useless
views.case: The questions in verses 2 to 5 say the wood is useless 'even when it was whole.' Some read this as an argument that Israel's value lay wholly in being God's planting, and had no independent worth. The vine has nothing to offer except fruit, and without it the entire plant is expendable.

views.label: For failing its purpose
views.case: Others stress verse 8, where the cause given is not the nature of the wood but the people's unfaithfulness. On this reading the parable is a vivid way of saying that a vine which does not bear fruit has no other reason to exist, and the fault lies in the failure to be what God planted it to be.

debates.bearing: The two views meet at the cross, since in both the vine's value is in the fruit that God's grace makes possible. The New Testament states the positive side, that fruit comes from remaining in Christ, John 15:5, and does not come from the branch's own resources.

study.originalLanguages:
The first word to notice is gephen, vine, and the wood it is compared to, 'ets, which is the general word for tree and timber. The question in verse 2 asks how the wood of the vine 'surpasses' other wood; the Hebrew is a comparison, and the answer implied is that it does not. In verse 3 the 'peg,' yated, is the same word used for a tent peg, as in Judges 4:21 where Jael drives one through Sisera's temple, and for the peg in Isaiah 22:23 on which a household's honor hangs. The vine cannot supply even this small thing, to carry any vessel, kli. The contrast between a peg that can bear a load and wood that bears nothing is the sharpness of the question.

The fire 'devours both ends.' The Hebrew speaks of the fire 'eating,' the verb akhal, and the word translated 'fuel' in verses 4 and 6 is a noun from the same root, okhlah, literally 'for eating' or 'for food.' The wood is given to the fire as the fire's meal. The picture is of the vine as a consumable, and verse 6 says God Himself has 'given' it to the fire. The verb is natan, the plain word for giving, which makes the act deliberate.

Verse 5 contains the key adjective, tamim, translated 'whole.' It is the word for something complete, intact and sound, and it is applied elsewhere to blameless persons and flawless offerings. Ezekiel is using it of the vine in its undamaged state, a vine that has not been burned, and saying that even in that condition it could not be made into anything. The statement is aimed at the people's assumption that a better state, before the disasters, would have been worth something.

In verses 7 and 8 the repeated 'I will set My face against them' uses the idiom of directing one's face toward someone to oppose, which Ezekiel uses often. In Ezekiel 14:8 the same expression was used of the idolater. Face is the opposite of the blessing of Numbers 6:25-26 in which the LORD makes His face shine on His people. The final noun, ma'al, 'unfaithfully,' is the word the chapter ends on, and it is the same root that Ezekiel 14:13 used, 'acting unfaithfully,' with the infinitive doubled. The two chapters are chained by the one idea. Ma'al is the language of a trust violated, used in Leviticus 5:15 for misusing what is holy to the LORD. The land becomes desolate, shemamah, because Israel misused what had been consecrated to God.

typology.type: The vine that bears no fruit, Ezekiel 15:2-6
typology.fulfillment: Ezekiel's useless vine finds its immediate correspondence in the fig tree that Jesus found with leaves but no fruit, Matthew 21:19, and in the tree that is cut down for not bearing, Luke 13:6-9. The correspondence deepens in John 15, where the unfruitful branch is 'thrown away and withers' and gathered 'into the fire,' verse 6. In Christ the type is escalated from a nation to the individual, and from judgment alone to the choice of remaining or not remaining in Him. The type falls short in that Ezekiel's vine is Jerusalem with no other source, while John 15 introduces the true vine as the one source of life.

typology.type: The vine as God's people, Ezekiel 15:6
typology.fulfillment: Israel is God's planting, Isaiah 5:7, and the vine of Psalm 80. Jesus claims the title for Himself, 'I am the true vine,' John 15:1, as the faithful Israel in whom God's people are gathered. Paul describes the church as grafted branches in an olive tree, Romans 11:17, and warns them against the arrogance that led Israel astray, 11:20-22. The correspondence is that the people of God are defined by fruit. The type is incomplete because the fruitfulness of the true vine is Christ's own, supplied by Him to branches that remain in Him, Galatians 5:22.

typology.type: The firebrand snatched from the fire, Ezekiel 15:7
typology.fulfillment: The people who have 'escaped the fire' only to face another recall the image of Zechariah 3:2, 'a firebrand snatched from the fire,' and Amos 4:11, where Israel was like a firebrand snatched from a blaze and yet did not return. Both show rescue that was meant to lead to repentance. The New Testament sets the final rescue in Christ, who delivers believers from the wrath to come, 1 Thessalonians 1:10. The type is limited because those who escaped in 597 were not changed by the escape, while those delivered in Christ are made new.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ by contrast and by promise. The contrast is the sharpest in the whole stretch of chapters, since Ezekiel declares that the vine is good for nothing, and John 15 answers with a vine that is good for everything. Jesus says, 'I am the true vine, and My Father is the keeper of the vineyard,' John 15:1. The adjective 'true' does not mean the earlier vine was false but that it was a shadow of the real thing, the faithful Israel in whom the vine's purpose is finally accomplished. Isaiah 5 tells of a vineyard that yields sour fruit; in Jesus the vineyard at last yields what God looked for.

It leads to Christ by the nature of fruit. Ezekiel's point is that vine wood has value only for its fruit. The New Testament shows where the fruit comes from: 'The one who remains in Me, and I in him, will bear much fruit. For apart from Me you can do nothing,' John 15:5. The branches of Ezekiel 15 had no source in themselves, and neither do the branches of John 15. What Israel tried to produce on its own, Christ produces in His people through the Spirit, whose fruit is love, joy, peace and the rest, Galatians 5:22, and 'the fruit of righteousness that comes through Jesus Christ,' Philippians 1:11.

It leads to Christ by His taking the fire. Ezekiel says God gives the vine to the fire as fuel. At the cross the true vine was cast out and burned in the place of the branches. Isaiah 53 describes Him as a root out of dry ground, and 53:5 says He was pierced for our transgressions. He bore the judgment that the fruitless vine deserved, so that those who are in Him need not bear it. Hebrews 6:7-8 warns that land that produces thorns is burned, and John 15:2 says the Father prunes the fruitful branch so that it bears more. Judgment and pruning come from the same hand.

It leads to Christ finally by the hope of a restored vine. Isaiah 27:2-3 sings of a fruitful vineyard that the LORD guards night and day, and Ezekiel 17:22-23 promises a tender shoot planted on the mountain heights of Israel that will bear fruit and become a majestic cedar. The New Testament sees that shoot in Jesus, the Branch of Isaiah 11:1.

A word of care: nothing in Ezekiel 15 is a coded picture of Jesus. The wood, the peg and the fire are parts of one parable about Jerusalem. The link is that Jesus takes up the vine image of the prophets and places Himself at its center, and the passage gives the problem that He answers, which is a people without fruit and without hope of producing it.
study.god:
The first thing the chapter shows is a God who is not impressed by status. In verse 2 He asks Ezekiel how the vine's wood is any better than other wood, and the question reveals that He does not rank His people by their position. He chose Israel, Deuteronomy 7:7-8 says, out of love and not because of any greatness, and that same freedom means He is not bound to protect a people who have abandoned the purpose of the choice. His faithfulness to His own covenant is not the same as sentimentality about His people.

It shows a God who looks for fruit. Isaiah 5:2 says He waited for the vineyard to yield good grapes, and the sour fruit moved Him to action. He is not indifferent to what His people do. Righteousness and justice are the fruit He seeks, Isaiah 5:7, and He holds His people accountable for producing them. This is the same God who plants, waters and guards, Isaiah 27:2-3, so His expectation is not harsh; it is what any gardener expects of a planting he has tended.

It shows a God who is the judge and not merely the observer of the judgment. In verse 6 He says, 'which I have given to the fire.' The Babylonian army was the instrument, but God claims the act. Jeremiah 52:13 reports the burning, and Ezekiel tells us beforehand who gave the order. The same truth that makes the judgment terrifying also makes it purposeful, since the God who burns is the God who has said what He will do and why.

It shows that God's judgments are repeated and progressive. The fire of 597 was not enough, verse 7, and 'another fire' follows. The Lord had been patient, and chapters 13 and 14 show Him sending warnings and calls to repent. Romans 2:4 says that His kindness is meant to lead to repentance, and a delay used badly stores up the judgment that comes.

It shows a God who sets His face. The phrase 'I will set My face against them,' verse 7, is the dark reversal of the blessing in which He makes His face shine on His people, Numbers 6:25. The God who delights to look on His people with favor turns His gaze the other way when they betray Him, and the prospect is the most severe in the chapter.

And it shows God as the keeper of the vine in the New Testament, who prunes the branches that bear fruit, John 15:2. Taken together, the God of Ezekiel 15 is the God who is just to the unfruitful and generous to those who remain. For worship, the response is not to claim a standing but to ask for fruit, to remain in the vine, and to thank the Father who has planted us.

crossReferences.note: Israel as a vine brought out of Egypt, planted in the land, and then cut down and burned. The psalm pleads for the vine's restoration, and Ezekiel answers that the burning is the vine's own doing. It shows the memory that Ezekiel was turning against the people's pride.

The love song of the vineyard, where God looked for good grapes and found sour ones, and so removes its hedge and wall. It states the principle behind Ezekiel 15: the point of planting is fruit, and the vineyard of the LORD of Hosts is the house of Israel.

God planted a choice vine from the very best seed and asks how it turned into a rotten, wild vine. It is the earlier prophetic counterpart to Ezekiel's question, and it places the failure in what the vine became and not in what God made.

Israel was a luxuriant vine whose fruit increased the more it increased its altars. Prosperity fed idolatry rather than gratitude, which explains why a vine that bears fruit only for itself and its other gods is judged.

Ezekiel returns to the vine, now as a spreading vine of low height planted in fertile soil, standing for Judah under Babylon. It carries the parable of chapter 15 into the politics of Zedekiah's reign.

A lament for a vine that was fruitful by abundant waters and then uprooted, its branches stripped and consumed by fire, with no strong branch left fit for a ruler's scepter. It shows the vine image carrying the end of the Davidic line's rule.

The people of Jerusalem say of the exiles that they are far from the LORD and that the land has been given to those who remain. It is the claim that the parable of the vine, with its second fire, is meant to overthrow.

Joshua the high priest is a firebrand snatched from the fire. The image gives a counterpoint to Ezekiel 15:7, showing that a rescue from burning can be a sign of mercy and a call to change, not a promise of safety.

Jesus tells of a landowner's vineyard rented to tenants who refuse to give its fruit, and says that the kingdom will be taken from them and given to a people who produce its fruit. He applies the vine tradition of Ezekiel and Isaiah to the leaders of His own day.

Jesus is the true vine, the Father is the keeper of the vineyard, and the branches that bear no fruit are thrown away and burned. Where Ezekiel announced the failure of the old vine, Jesus gives the way fruit comes, by remaining in Him.

study.oneStory:
Ezekiel 15 belongs to the long account of what the garden of Eden was meant to produce and what has gone wrong. God's purposes in creation were fruitful: 'be fruitful and multiply,' Genesis 1:28, and the garden he planted had trees good for food. The fall, Genesis 3, introduced thorns and thistles in place of fruit. From then on Scripture follows a planting that is meant to bear and a ground that resists. Ezekiel's vine is Israel in the position of the first man, planted by God, given everything, and expected to bear, who yet fails.

The passage answers, from before, the question of what Israel's election was for. God did not choose a nation to be admired but to bear fruit for the world, as He promised Abraham, 'all the families of the earth will be blessed through you,' Genesis 12:3. A vine that bears for no one has lost its reason for being. The prophets then trace the failure: Isaiah's sour grapes, Jeremiah's wild vine, Hosea's altars, and Ezekiel's wood good only for fuel. Ezekiel 15 is the verdict at the end of that line.

It also sets up what comes after. If the vine is burned, what is left? The prophets give the answer in promises of a new planting. Isaiah says, 'In that day, sing about a fruitful vineyard,' Isaiah 27:2, and Ezekiel 17:22-23 promises a tender shoot that will bear fruit. Jeremiah says the days are coming for a new covenant, Jeremiah 31:31. The chapter's severity makes room for a planting that does not rely on the old vine's own strength.

The story comes to rest in Jesus, who is the true vine and who invites His disciples to remain in Him and bear much fruit, John 15:5. The people of God, the church, are grafted into this root, Romans 11:17, and are to bear the fruit of the Spirit, Galatians 5:22. The old failure becomes a warning, in the same letter that gives the promise, Romans 11:20-22. And Jesus bore the fire for His people, so that the branches in Him are pruned, not burned.

The story ends in the new creation, where the curse of thorns and thistles is gone. The tree of life stands in the city, 'bearing twelve kinds of fruit and yielding a fresh crop for each month,' Revelation 22:2. The garden that began with a command to bear fruit ends with a fruitfulness that never fails. Ezekiel's charred wood is answered by a tree whose leaves heal the nations.

quiz.q: According to Ezekiel 15:2-3, how does the wood of a vine compare to timber from a forest tree?

options.text: It has no comparable use; it cannot even be made into a simple peg.
options.note: Verses 2-3 make this exact point through rhetorical questions expecting a negative answer.

options.text: It is stronger and more valuable than any other wood.
options.note: The passage argues the opposite: vine wood has no structural value at all.

options.text: It is equally useful for building houses.
options.note: The text explicitly denies the vine wood any building use.

options.text: It is prized mainly for its beautiful grain.
options.note: No aesthetic value is mentioned; the point is its lack of practical usefulness.

quiz.q: What is the vine's wood good for, according to this passage?

options.text: Only for fuel, being cast into the fire.
options.note: Verse 4 states the wood is cast into the fire for fuel, its only remaining use once it is not bearing fruit.

options.text: For making fine furniture.
options.note: The passage denies any refined or practical use for the wood itself.

options.text: For crafting tools and pegs.
options.note: Verse 3 explicitly denies this exact use.

options.text: For decorative garden trellises.
options.note: No such use is mentioned; the text focuses narrowly on fuel as the wood's only remaining purpose.

quiz.q: To whom does God directly apply the image of the useless, charred vine wood?

options.text: The people of Jerusalem.
options.note: Verse 6 states plainly, 'so I will give up the people of Jerusalem.'

options.text: The nations surrounding Israel.
options.note: The application is specifically and directly to Jerusalem, not the surrounding nations.

options.text: Only the false prophets described in the previous chapters.
options.note: The application is to the people of Jerusalem generally, not narrowly to the false prophets.

options.text: The exiles already living in Babylon.
options.note: The judgment described is specifically against Jerusalem and its inhabitants, not the exiled community receiving the message.

quiz.q: What does verse 7 mean by saying, 'though they may have escaped the fire, yet another fire will consume them'?

options.text: Even those who survived an earlier judgment will face a further, complete judgment.
options.note: This reflects the wood's charred condition from an earlier fire, now facing complete consumption by a second, decisive fire.

options.text: God promises complete protection from any future disaster.
options.note: The verse warns of further judgment, not protection from it.

options.text: The fire refers only to a literal accidental fire in Jerusalem's history.
options.note: The fire is figurative, representing God's ongoing judgment, not a literal historical accident.

options.text: It promises that no further judgment will ever come upon the people.
options.note: The verse promises the opposite, a further and more complete judgment still to come.

quiz.q: What underlying reason does God give in verse 8 for making the land desolate?

options.text: Because the people acted unfaithfully, a direct covenant betrayal.
options.note: Verse 8 explicitly names 'they have acted unfaithfully' as the reason for the coming desolation.

options.text: Because the land itself was naturally unproductive.
options.note: The desolation is judgment for unfaithfulness, not a natural agricultural deficiency.

options.text: Because foreign armies simply happened to invade.
options.note: The desolation is presented as God's direct judgment for unfaithfulness, not incidental to foreign invasion alone.

options.text: Because the people had grown too numerous for the land to support.
options.note: Overpopulation is not the stated reason; covenant unfaithfulness is.

questions: Israel took comfort in being God's vine without bearing fruit to match that identity. What privileges or labels, being part of a church, a Christian family, or a long history of faith, might you be leaning on instead of actually bearing fruit?
The vine's wood has no independent value apart from fruit. Where in your life have you confused having a good reputation or position with actually producing the fruit of a transformed life?

Jerusalem had already been scorched by one judgment yet still bore no fruit, inviting a second, greater fire. What warnings or hardships in your own life might God be using to call you toward repentance before something more serious follows?

Jesus reclaims this exact image, calling Himself the true vine whose branches bear real fruit only by abiding in Him. What practical habits help you stay abiding in Christ this week rather than trying to bear fruit through your own effort?

This parable is unsentimental about privilege without fruitfulness. Where might you need to let go of assuming God's favor is automatic, and instead ask honestly whether your life is bearing the fruit that identity implies?

translationNotes.note: The rhetorical question 'how does the wood of the vine surpass any other branch' expects the answer 'it does not', setting up the parable's entire argument that vine wood has no independent structural value.

The description of the fire devouring 'both ends' while the 'middle is charred' pictures a piece of vine wood already partially burned as kindling, useless even before any further fire comes, intensifying the image of total worthlessness.

The term rendered 'acted unfaithfully' carries the sense of a serious breach of trust or covenant betrayal, the same root used throughout the Old Testament for grave unfaithfulness to God, not a minor or accidental lapse.
